definition: A named place in memory that holds a value your program can read and change.
The kind of data a variable holds, which sets how many bytes it uses and how those bytes are read.
A line that tells the compiler a name exists and what type it has.
Giving a variable its first value at the moment it is created.
Replacing the value a variable already holds, using the = operator.
A whole number with no decimal part, stored in C++ as an int or a similar type.
A way of storing numbers with decimal parts, close to the real value but not always exact.
A value that is either true or false, stored in C++ as a bool.
A one-byte type that holds a single character, stored as its numeric code.
An integer type that can hold negative and positive values.
An integer type that holds only zero and positive values, which gives it a larger top end for the same number of bytes.
What happens when a result is too large for its type to hold, so the stored value is wrong.
A named value that cannot change after it is set, marked with const.
The part of a program where a name can be used, usually the braces it was declared inside.
A variable declared inside a function or block, which exists only until that block ends.
A variable declared outside every function, which any later code in the file can use.
A C++ operator that gives how many bytes a type or variable takes up.
A variable created without a value, which holds whatever was already in its memory.
A value written directly in code, like 42, 3.25 or true.
A piece of code that works out to a single value, like speed * 2 + 1.
A symbol that does something to values, like + or ==.
A value an operator works on, like the 2 and 3 in 2 + 3.
Division between two integers, which throws away the fractional part of the answer.
The % operator, which gives the remainder after integer division.
The rules for which operators in an expression run first, like * before +.
Code that deliberately converts a value from one type to another, like static_cast<double>(x).
A type conversion the compiler does on its own, without you asking for it in code.
The tiny difference between a real number and the nearest value a floating-point type can store.
An expression that works out to true or false, used to decide what code runs.
An operator that compares two values and gives true or false, like < or ==.
An operator that combines true and false values: && for and, || for or, ! for not.
Skipping the right side of && or || when the left side has already settled the answer.
A point where a program picks which code to run next, or one of the paths it can pick.
A fixed number of values of one type, stored side by side in memory under one name.
One value inside an array.
The number that picks an element of an array, written in square brackets.
Counting positions from 0, so the first element of an array is at index 0.
Using an index outside an array, which reaches memory that belongs to something else.
Code that runs repeatedly while a condition stays true.
One run through the body of a loop.
A loop whose condition never becomes false, so it runs until something stops the program.
The expression a loop checks to decide whether to run again.
A bug where a loop or index is wrong by exactly one, often from using <= where < belongs.
A loop inside the body of another loop, where the inner one runs fully for each outer iteration.
Writing past the end of an array, which overwrites whatever happens to sit next to it in memory.
A named block of code that can be run from anywhere by calling it.
A variable in a function definition that receives a value when the function is called.
The actual value passed to a function when calling it.
The value a function hands back to the code that called it.
Running a function: the program jumps to it, runs it, then comes back.
A line giving a function's name, return type and parameters, without its body.
A function's name and parameter types, which is what the compiler uses to tell functions apart.
Giving a function its own copy of an argument, so changes inside don't reach the caller.
Writing several functions with the same name but different parameter types.
The memory that tracks which functions are running, with one stack frame per active call.
The block of stack memory for one function call, holding its parameters, local variables and where to return to.
Running out of stack memory, usually from calls nested too deeply.
A function calling itself, usually on a smaller version of the same problem.
Hiding how something works behind a simple name, so you can use it without thinking about its details.
A function that returns nothing, marked with the return type void.
A variable whose value is a memory address.
Following a pointer to reach the value at the address it holds, written with *.
The & operator, which gives the memory address of a variable.
A pointer that holds no valid address, written nullptr in C++.
A second name for an existing variable, declared with & after the type.
Giving a function access to the caller's own variable, so changes inside reach the caller.
A reference that can read a variable but not change it, often used to avoid copying large values.
A region of memory where a program can request space at any time and keep it until it gives it back.
The region of memory holding local variables and function calls, freed automatically as functions return.
Requesting memory from the heap while the program runs, with new in C++.
Heap memory that is never given back, usually because the pointer to it was lost.
A pointer to memory that has already been freed or has gone out of scope.
A crash caused by a program touching memory it isn't allowed to use.
